If Caelus could give himself a title besides Galactic Baseballer, Trailblazer, and He With The Shittiest Gacha Luck, he thinks he’d call himself the Galaxy’s Most Pitiful Third Wheeler To Ever Wheel.

He knew that his luck was bad in Belobog. It got worse, somehow, in the Luofu—probably because he was third wheeling three people (fourth-wheeling?), but only one of the three actually remembered the relationship. So he was thankful when he did very little third-wheeling in Penacony—probably since they had the more pressing issue of Sunday attempting to rewrite an entire reality looming over their heads.

Caelus thinks that any normal person, after wheeling as hard as he has on three different planets, would hope that the next destination would have no ‘rivals to lovers’ or ‘doomed yaoi’ or even ‘eyefucking’ (the latter, in particular, is something that even he with his brazenness had no idea how to deal with). He’s begged this to the Aeons out there, and then to Pom-Pom, and then to the doleful eyes of March’s plushies while she laughed at him.

So when Caelus sits through two whole hours of Mydei and Phainon bickering and giving each other heated gazes when they think the other isn’t looking, he thinks, in order: not again and how the fuck are these two even worse than all the others and did Kafka bring me into this universe to become its third wheel or something, before immediately dragging Dan Heng away to discuss.

“So,” Caelus says, sat cross-legged in the bedroom that Aglaea had gifted to them, hope brimming in his Stellaron-ridden heart.

Dan Heng glances at him, takes one look at his trusty whiteboard, and promptly turns his back.

“No.”

“You haven’t even heard me out!” Caelus protests.

“The answer is still no,” Dan Heng says. He crosses his arms. “Your whiteboard has never yielded anything positive.”

“Okay, first off, that’s a lie, because you like my ideas and you know it,” Caelus counters. “Secondly, this is a serious matter, and it requires both of us. I can’t do it alone.” He places a hand piously on his heart, Sunday-style. “I solemnly swear this on the twelve long months of life I’ve lived thus far.”

Dan Heng ignores him, so Caelus tries a different tack. “I swear on every trashcan in Amphoreus.”

“There are no trashcans in Amphoreus,” Dan Heng finally sighs. It’s long-suffering and familiar, and Caelus loves it so. “Fine. What are you proposing this time?”

Wordlessly, Caelus flips the whiteboard. Dan Heng peers at it, brows furrowing.

To his credit, he does properly scrutinise the thing. Caelus assumed he’d take one look at the heading and refuse to read the rest.

Still, Dan Heng’s conclusion is—

“No.”

“Please,” Caelus wheedles. “Dan Heng, hear me out. I can’t do this anymore. First it was Bronya and Seele, and whatever they had going on, which—fine, it was sweet, but I was two months old and didn’t really get it until Natasha pulled me aside and explained it to me. Which was mortifying, by the way.”

Dan Heng looks like he wants to interrupt, so Caelus puts a finger on his lips. His eyes go adorably cross-eyed. Cute.

“You weren’t here for this, but I also had to sit through Acheron and Black Swan and their constant tension and it kind of felt like being in the middle of a weird dance, except I was the floor getting stepped on.” Dan Heng looks at him reproachfully, so Caelus moves his finger away. “And of course, there was you and Jing Yuan—”

“What,” Dan Heng sputters.

“And Blade, too, now that I think about it—”

“Caelus—”

“—but these two,” Caelus groans, flopping backwards onto the floor, “are somehow worse than all of them combined.”

He truly can’t take it anymore. In no universe should he have to witness Mydei’s hand linger on Phainon’s shoulder for a moment longer than what two friends consider proper, and then watch as Mydei flexes his hand right afterwards, clearly so affected by it. Like something straight out of March’s romance novels.

Seriously, Phainon’s eyes had softened when he looked at Mydei. Multiple times. In public! And here Caelus thought eyes could only soften in Jing Yuan fanfiction.

Dan Heng gives him a look. “Phainon and Mydei are good friends. They’re bound to bicker every once in a while.”

Caelus sits up, wholly indignant. “Have you seen them,” he demands.

“I have, yes.”

Evidently Dan Heng hasn’t, if he still thinks that they’re only good friends.

Caelus grabs his pen, and nearly stabs the whiteboard in his haste to draw up a bullet point list. A blotch of ink lands on his sleeve, but he doesn’t care.

“When we first met, Mydei only spoke to Phainon, because he literally didn’t even register that we were there, even though we were right in front of him,” Caelus stresses. Bullet point one. “Phainon made me run up a whole electrified stairway just to race Mydei.” Bullet point two. “One in three of our conversations with Phainon involve Mydei. Trust me, I counted them and worked out the average.” Bullet point three. And, for the final, decisive stroke: “They stare at each other’s lips even when I’m right there but I’m too short to do anything about it so really, I’m just standing there staring up at their tits the whole time. While they flirt with each other. Like I’m not even there.”

Dan Heng pauses. “Are you… jealous?” he asks, mouth pursed.

Caelus blinks at him. “What? No, definitely not.” Objectively, they’re hot, but he’s not interested. “I just need to get rid of this ‘Doomed Third Wheel’ curse, because otherwise it’ll probably follow me into the next planet. And then I’d have to die, because there’s only so much one guy can take.”

For some reason, Dan Heng visibly relaxes. “You won’t be dying any time soon,” he says, seriously. “And while perhaps Mydei and Phainon are closer than most friends, whether or not they’re more than that is hardly any of our business.”

“Do close friends bathe together?” Caelus asks, seriously. “Like that?”

Dan Heng opens his mouth, considers, and then closes his mouth. He looks slightly mollified.

Bingo. Now for the hook, line, and…

“I just don’t want to be a third wheel anymore,” Caelus despairs. He flutters his lashes. This is bound to work. “Is that so much to ask for?”

“You’re not a third wheel,” Dan Heng tells him, unimpressed.

Flutter, flutter. “March wouldn’t do this to me,” Caelus whines.

Dan Heng, the cheater, turns away from him. “If there truly is something going on between them, then we shouldn’t interfere. They deserve their privacy.”

He said ‘we’, not ‘you’, Caelus thinks hopefully, before Dan Heng casually crushes his hopes by settling into his lounge chair and taking out a book.

No amount of badgering gets him to budge. Caelus slinks back to his whiteboard, and mournfully erases his list.

Fine. He doesn’t need Dan Heng’s help. He can just… wait until Dan Heng decides to help him of his own accord (and he definitely will, because Dan Heng can never leave him to his own devices for too long before he starts to worry, since he’s sweet like that). Caelus just has to pester him some more until he gives in.

Until then, Caelus can make a plan.

He uncaps his pen.

CAELUS AND DAN HENG’S

“Leave my name out of it,” Dan Heng says, flipping the page of his book without even looking at the whiteboard.

“Boo,” Caelus grumbles.

Phainon strides into the training grounds. He looks around for a moment, confused, before brightening up (like a puppy, Caelus thinks) when his gaze lands on the only other occupant in the area.

“Mydei!” Phainon calls, brightly. “You wouldn’t happen to have seen the Trailblazer around here, would you?”

Mydei turns around, and regards Phainon with a curious look. “No. I was looking for him myself,” he says. “He invited me to a spar.”

“Strange. He invited me to a spar, too,” Phainon says. He raises an eyebrow, and grins. “Looks like one of us got our schedules mixed up. Forgetting things in your old age, Mydei?”

Mydei crosses his arms. If Caelus squints, he can just about make out the vein in his forehead pulsing.

“I’m immortal, not an invalid,” Mydei retorts. “And you’re one to talk, Deliverer. I recall that you couldn’t remember a single date in our history lessons. Are you sure that your memory isn’t so atrocious that you simply forgot your appointment?”

Phainon places a hand on his chest, mock-offended. “Hey, what do my academics have to do with this?” he complains. “I could very well say that you probably got your appointment wrong, given your abysmal mathematics. Did you ever learn to read the time in the end, Mydei, or is that skill still beyond you?”

Even from this distance, the fondness in Phainon’s sly smile is striking. Still, Caelus manages to pinpoint the exact moment that the vein in Mydei’s head figuratively pops.

“Enough of this,” Mydei growls. He shifts into a fighting stance, feet set squarely apart and fists raised. “Why don’t we settle this here, fair and square?”

At that, Phainon throws his head back and laughs. It's a relaxed, carefree sound. Almost boyish, even, in a way that Caelus hasn’t quite heard from Phainon before.

“Your words are music to my ears,” Phainon promises, before he summons his blade.

Oh shit, Caelus thinks. He ducks behind the column, right before a resounding boom reverberates through the training grounds, the force of it nearly throwing him into the air and crashing into the opposite street.

And thus begins the world’s most protracted form of foreplay.

Caelus rubs his hands together eagerly. If all goes to plan, by the end of today there’ll be one more couple walking around Okhema, and he will finally be able to rest.

All does not go to plan.

It’s been over two hours. Caelus’ legs are going numb, his trusty column is about to crumble, and he’s starting to suspect that the only reason he hasn’t been found out yet is because Mydei and Phainon have tunnel vision for each other, and the peripheral vision of a dromas for anyone else.

The pair trade blows in the skilful way that only those that know each other intimately do. Caelus watches, mostly tired but also fascinated, as Mydei caves craters into the floor with his indomitable strength, and as Phainon swiftly dodges his blows, only to return them with equal fervour. The ease with which they respond to each other feels almost like watching a pair of birds in flight, or the push-pull of the tide and the moon. Caelus thinks that he’s never seen anything like it.

Neither of them have stayed their attacks, even for a second. The intensity in their gazes, trained wholly on each other, makes Caelus almost feel like he’s intruding.

Carefully, Caelus peeks around the column. The sight almost makes him weep.

Phainon is laughing again. He’s loud, genuine, and wild, teeth bared and eyes blazing—even when Mydei grabs him by the collar and slams him into the ground.

“I win,” Mydei says, smugly. He shifts, looming over Phainon like a dark shadow, and— okay, now he’s straddling Phainon’s waist and physically pinning him to the ground. “Enlighten me, Deliverer. What’s the score now?”

Beneath Mydei, Phainon’s chest heaves. His shirt is riding up, soaked with sweat and revealing a swathe of skin. He’s gazing at Mydei, mouth parted, and Caelus is sure that his eyes are dilated.

The look of love, Caelus thinks, wistfully. If only he was closer to confirm it for himself.

“Who knows?” Phainon says, breathlessly. “I wouldn’t count your victory quite so soon, Mydei.”

There’s a flash of movement. Before Mydei can respond, Phainon places a hand on his bare waist, and squeezes.

Mydei freezes. The way his face contorts with shock is almost comical. His mouth makes an ‘O’ shape, and his cheeks redden rapidly. Phainon probably has no time to pray, so Caelus places a hand over his heart and sends a prayer up to Kephale for him.

“You and your conniving schemes,” Mydei snarls, going straight for Phainon’s throat.

Expertly, Phainon dodges. He leaps to his feet, and grins wolfishly. “What about them? They help even the odds against a man with your constitution, do they not—?”

Mydei pivots, picks up a nearby table, and launches it at Phainon’s head.

Luckily, Phainon ducks. Unluckily, Caelus has approximately half a second to realise that the table is headed his way before he can throw himself to the side, and watch, miserably, as it demolishes his trusty column.

Their match goes on for hours. By the end of it, Caelus’ eyes are drooping with fatigue, and even then the two of them are still going somehow.

He had really expected Phainon and Mydei to spar, press their sweaty bodies against each other and then hopefully make out. Instead, Mydei had been so focused on throttling Phainon that he didn’t even notice that he’d nearly beheaded Caelus with a table. Hell, Caelus wouldn’t be surprised if neither of them remembered their original reason for coming to the training grounds.

He doesn’t want to admit defeat. He really, really doesn’t want to admit defeat. But his eyes feel like someone glued them shut, and even he’s not delusional enough to pretend that this is going anywhere beyond—well. Homoerotic sparring.

Caelus sniffs, pathetically. March’s novels lied to him.

Surely, though, more good things will come to those who wait, and to those who get a full eight hours of sleep, background battle noises and manly yelling be damned.

So Caelus treks back to his and Dan Heng’s room. While he’s dragging his feet, he comes to realise, in order, three things:

1. The sparring-aka-foreplay is normal for them, and won’t change any time soon. 2. His methods need to be more direct. 3. But before that, he needs intel.

At least, Caelus thinks it’s his dinner. The substance in his bowl is as black as tar, with pieces of what looks like regurgitated cat food floating ominously on the surface.

Phainon laughs. “I may or may not have made a poor choice of wording earlier today,” he admits, “and compromised my only chance for a safe dinner. Caelus blinks. “Do you want me to get you something from the Diner?”

“No need,” Phainon tells him. He taps the substance with his fork. It actually belches at him. “I think that would actually piss him off more.”

Caelus doesn’t understand, but he presses on anyway.

Phainon cocks his head to the side. Like this, he almost looks like an adorable, overgrown puppy. “What brought this on?” he asks. “Is this about the food? Because if so, you should know that this isn’t a universal experience. Your dinner will remain safe and in capable hands, I swear.”

He trails off, because either his eyesight is playing tricks on him, or that’s Dan Heng lingering outside the window, softly petting a chimera perching on his head.

Caelus feels a rush of incredulity. Dan Heng won’t help him out, but he’ll still eavesdrop? For shame!

“Just that?” Phainon prompts.

Caelus shakes himself out of his stupor. As he does, an idea slowly begins to form in his head, and he has to suppress the urge to grin.

“It’s just that…  Dan Heng keeps up an archive,” he says, smoothly. “And he’s been getting… antsy, recently, because he normally documents everything we encounter on our travels, but for Mydei he’s got barely anything.”

Through the window, Dan Heng stiffens.

“It’s making him stressed,” Caelus lies. “He keeps pacing in our room. I fear that if he doesn’t get any information soon, he’ll start—stress-knitting, or something. And you really don’t want to see what he gets like when he starts stress-knitting.”

At that, Dan Heng turns around slowly. He gives Caelus a Look. The chimera on his head yawns, and curls up to sleep, like a little woollen hat.

Caelus laughs under his breath. Payback has never been so sweet.

Then, Phainon grins. “But that’s all the boring stuff. Let me tell you about the real Mydei.” He crooks a finger and beckons Caelus closer. Caelus leans in eagerly. “Mydei’s actually quite knowledgeable about flowers. He enjoys playing with children, and if there’s no one around, he’ll let them braid flowers into his hair.” Phainon’s expression grows fond. “He’s also a huge bookworm. You might not believe it if you judge him by first glance, but his historical knowledge is impressive. But he also enjoys reading other books—just the other day I found him reading a saucy novella that even the old ladies of Okhema would blush at. And he defended it!” He laughs. “Apparently, even badly written erotica makes for engaging social commentary if you indulge enough.

Phainon smiles at him knowingly. “My friend, it seems like you’re fishing for something.”

Oh, he’s definitely caught on. Fortunately, Caelus has covered all his bases.

He switches to the puppy eyes. “It’s for Dan Heng,” he explains, mouth purposefully wobbling. “I can’t go back to him empty handed. His disappointed face would break my heart.”

Phainon stares at him. Then, his eyes widen.

“Is that how it is? I see.” For some reason, he looks more at ease. He tilts his head back, and looks up at the sky. “Well, at risk of repeating myself, Mydei is a good friend and a worthy rival.” Then, more quietly: “He understands me better than I understand myself.”

With those profound parting words, Caelus thanks him and leaves. He wills himself to walk normally towards the exit, because the newfound knowledge of how deeply Phainon truly understands Mydei nearly has him skipping out of the dining hall in his glee.

When Caelus chances one last glance back, he catches Phainon gazing softly down at his dinner again. How poetic: to be so lovestruck that even a meal as nauseating as that can’t distract him from the object of his affections. Caelus notes this down with utmost approval.

This plan is becoming a resounding success, if he does say so himself.

Caelus finds Mydei brooding on a rooftop in Marmoreal Market.

He watches Caelus clamber up the stairs and huff and puff across the canopies with the same look one gives a dying rat in the depths of an alleyway. Once Caelus finally catches up to him, Mydei sighs.

“Usually, when someone stands alone, they do so for a reason,” he says, gruffly.

He still moves aside to make space for Caelus, though, so Caelus counts that as a win.

“Noted,” Caelus says, cheerily. “But I actually came here to talk to you about something important.”

Mydei inclines his head. “Go on.”

“I need your honest opinion on Phainon. For reasons.”

“And what would those reasons be?”

Like he’d done with Phainon, Caelus explains about Dang Heng and his data bank.

“I can’t go back without anything,” he says. “Dan Heng would be sad.”

That’s a lie. At worst, he’d probably just sulk, but Mydei doesn’t have to know that.

Mydei looks him up and down. It’s hard to tell what he’s thinking, because his brow is as furrowed as usual and he looks as serious as ever, but Caelus still puts on his most convincing ‘kicked-puppy’ look. It must work, because a strange look of understanding dawns on Mydei’s face, before he begins to speak.

“The Deliverer is a fool,” he says, slowly. “He always needs someone to watch his back. He may trust his heart to guide him, but if he doesn’t keep it in check, it will become his downfall.”

Caelus opens his mouth, confused, but Mydei interrupts him before he can say a word.

“He is also the only one capable of keeping up with me, and his skills are peerless. Okhema is as safe as it will ever be in his hands.”

Caelus closes his mouth, feeling strangely touched. He hadn’t been expecting such praise from Mydei—not outright, at least. He’d thought the process would be more like pulling a chew toy out of an angry dog’s mouth.

“Anything else?” he prompts.

Mydei levels him with a look that puts the fear of Nikador into his legs and turns them to jelly. “If you want to know more about him, you should ask him, instead of coming to me. Better yet, observe him in battle, or spar with him yourself.”

I don’t want to ask him, I want to ask YOU about him, Caelus wails, internally.

“Understood,” he says, instead.

Mydei turns his back on him, and Caelus takes that to be universal Mydei-speak for ‘I’m done here, go bother someone else’. And leave to bother another unlikely soul he does, until he remembers Phainon’s parting words to him in the dining hall.

Caelus turns on his heel. “Also, he says that he’s currently winning in your ‘current competition’?” he calls after Mydei, “whatever that means. Just thought I’d let you know.”

For a long moment, Mydei simply looks at him, gaze inscrutable. Caelus wonders whether his meddling really has gone too far.

Then, Mydei snorts, and mutters a word that Caelus doesn’t quite understand.

“He may be in the lead for now, but he won’t last long,” Mydei smirks. “I will overtake him eventually.”

Caelus leaves Mydei on that rooftop, watching as he gazes into the distance with a self-satisfied smile.

Dan Heng rounds on Caelus the minute he enters their room.

“I told you not to drag me into this,” Dan Heng says, exasperated. “And stress-knitting? Really? Of all things?”

“Sorry, I panicked,” Caelus apologises. He reaches out, and pats Dan Heng’s hand. “But I hardly dragged you into this because you were clearly listening in—don’t pretend you weren’t! And you can’t deny that we got crucial information out of those conversations.”

Dan Heng huffs, but he doesn’t deny the accusation. “And what were you planning to do with that information?”

“You’ll see,” Caelus winks. “Everything’s being set into motion. We just need to sit back and wait.”

Three days later, Caelus finds Mydei tenderly dressing Phainon’s wounds and scolding him angrily, while Phainon leans back into his chest and complains.

Caelus decides that he no longer has it in himself to wait.

Unlike you, the Trailblazer knows how to pick up a book and consolidate his own understanding of the topic.”

“I can touch them, right?” Caelus pleads, diverting the attention back onto himself. “Just once?”

Phainon’s free hand twitches. Can’t a man be curious? Caelus wants to ask him cheekily, but he holds his breath.

Mydei sighs, long-suffering. “Once,” he acquiesces. “Although I warn you that it feels no different to ordinary skin.”

Caelus cheers, and reaches out a hand. His fingers don’t even get to skim the hair on Mydei’s chest before Phainon’s caught his wrist in a vice-grip.

“Ah, that’s hardly fair,” Phainon says, still smiling. “Mydei’s conspicuous body is priceless, you know. It would hardly be appropriate if anyone could touch it any time they wanted.”

“Really?” Caelus grins. “Well, maybe you should do something about that. Before someone else does.”

Phainon’s eyes flash dangerously, and he throws Caelus a look of betrayal. His hand makes an aborted motion, almost like he wants to bodily drag Caelus from the clearing altogether.

Caelus remembers, then, that although Phainon is a friend that he’s riling up, he’s also an incredibly powerful Chrysos Heir who’s gone toe-to-toe with thousands of Titankin and won. He could probably toss Caelus over the side of Okhema like a sack of potatoes if he wanted.

Ah, well. Caelus rolls his shoulder, and grins.

He’s the Galactic Baseballer. Putting his life on the front line is part of his daily routine. Anything for the rivals to lovers, and all that.

“What’s going on?”

Caelus whips around, and finds Dan Heng striding quickly towards them, his face drawn in confusion. He frowns. Since when did Dan Heng approach so quietly?

“Dan Heng!” Caelus says, surprised. He wonders whether he should explain, since Dan Heng isn’t in on this particular plan, but eventually settles on: fuck it, I may as well go all in. “I’m going to touch Mydei’s body.”

With any luck, Phainon will now attempt to kill him, OR yank Mydei back and growl possessively like a dog, OR sweep him into a kiss in front of all of Okhema to make a statement. Caelus isn’t picky. Any will do.

“What,” Mydei sputters, flustered.

“What,” Phainon snarls, gripping Mydei’s waist like a lifeline.

“What.”

Caelus startles, and turns to the source of the last voice. The sight nearly makes him jump.

Dan Heng’s face is decidedly sour. His eyes have narrowed into slits, and he’s staring at Caelus like he’s drinking in the sight of him for the first time in a long time, yet also like he wants Caelus to be as far away from here as possible.

Caelus wracks his brain for answers. Why is Dan Heng angry? He isn’t even supposed to be here, and while it’s still not too late to ask him to join in and help, Dan Heng has no idea what the plan is—

“Care to explain?” Dan Heng asks him, frostily.

Caelus wrings his hands, suddenly nervous. “Uh—well. I was asking about Mydei’s tattoos.” Caelus says, lamely. His voice comes out more of a squeak.

Somehow, he feels like he’s done something wrong. But he can’t fathom what it could be, and now the plan’s going awry because of it.

Mydei looks between the three of them, mouth pursed. A look of understanding crosses his face. He presses a palm to his forehead, and turns away.

“Whatever’s going on, leave me out of it. I want no part in this farce.”

The tension in Phainon’s shoulders bleeds out, and he pulls Mydei closer to him. “I agree completely,” he says, voice smooth. “Let’s stop this before it goes any further.”

Noooo, Caelus wants to cry, I was so close!

Dan Heng turns to Phainon. “In that case, please let go of Caelus,” he says. His tone indicates that it isn’t a request.

Phainon looks between the two of them, considering. Then, he looks at Mydei. The corner of Mydei’s mouth twitches. Phainon raises an eyebrow in question, and Mydei shrugs a response, which makes Phainon erupt into a shit-eating grin.

Since when could they use telepathy, Caelus thinks, actually impressed—right before Phainon suddenly lets go of Caelus’ wrist, interlocks their fingers, and yanks him forward so far that he nearly crashes into Phainon’s chest.

“I find I rather like it here, actually,” Phainon announces.

Caelus blinks. He sighs, and gives Phainon a deadpan look. Phainon only shrugs at him, before leaning in close. His breath skims hot against the shell of Caelus’ ear.

“Two can play at that game,” he murmurs, voice mischievous.

Caelus rolls his eyes. Whatever. He still managed to prove one of his hypotheses, at least. This just means he’ll have to return to the whiteboard again. It’s no big deal in the long run.

“Come on Dan Heng, let’s get going,” he says. There’s no response. “Dan Heng?”

Frowning at the silence, Caelus looks back—

—only to find Dan Heng staring at the place where his and Phainon’s hands are joined, looking downright murderous.

Oh no.

In an instant, Caelus’ priority shifts. Abort mission, abort mission—please don’t shift into your dragon form, Caelus begs. The wind is already picking up angrily around Dan Heng’s heels. If Caelus squints, he can definitely make out a teal glow around Dan Heng’s tense shoulders, threatening to burst forth and blind everyone in a five-mile radius if they don’t get going right now.

It would be really bad if Dan Heng’s tail came out and wrapped itself around Caelus’ leg again, or if it started storming here, in the land of perpetual daylight, or if he called down the whole of the Xianzhou Alliance to nuke one man.

Not that he would ever do that. He’s far too sensible.

Caelus looks at Dan Heng, and reconsiders his statement.

He yanks his hand out of Phainon’s grip, and hurriedly drags Dan Heng away. “Thanks for the history lesson, Mydei!” he calls, panicked. “I’ll record everything in the data bank!”

Later, Phainon catches up to him, looking every inch like a kicked puppy.

“I really am sorry,” he apologises, profusely. “I don’t know what came over me.”

Caelus waves him off. “Nah, it’s fine. All’s fair in love and war.”

Phainon flushes. “Still, what you saw was a rather—ugly side of me, that no friend should have had to see. I’m sorry for that.”

“I told you, it’s okay. Honestly, it was kind of funny.”

At that, Phainon smiles, looking relieved. “Well, I am grateful to have gained your forgiveness. Should I ever behave like that again, you have my permission to smack the foolishness out of me. Mydei’s words, not mine.” He looks around. “I also have to apologise to Dan Heng. I was trying to help him, but I realise that my method was completely out of order.”

“Ah…” Caelus trails off awkwardly. How can you explain the concept of an overprotective dragon to someone who has never seen a dragon before? “Maybe come back tomorrow?”

“Understood,” Phainon nods. He draws himself up to his full height, suddenly serious. “I will apologise on his terms. Like a man.”

Caelus frowns after him. Weird, but okay.

After Phainon’s trial and the incident at the Grove, Caelus barely has any time to create more steps for his plan. But he hasn’t forgotten about it. He can’t forget about it—not after he watches as Phainon’s expression melts into unguarded relief when Mydei enters the fray against the Flame Reaver, and the two of them seamlessly guard each other’s backs with the ferocity and desperation of devotion unending.

Caelus actually thinks that maybe, just maybe, they’ll confess their feelings organically, and he can finally lay down the hatchet.

Then, Mydei drops the worst bombshell known to man.

CAELUS’ AND DAN HENG’S INFALLIBLE 10 STEP PLAN TO STOP BEING A THIRD WHEEL GET PHAINON AND MYDEI TOGETHER BEFORE A) CAELUS GOES CRAZY B)

THEY DIE C) BOTH???

Get them to talk about their feelings too slow 3. 7 mins in amphorean heaven more like 7 mins in amphorean hell 4. date #2 ❌❌❌ i give up. Going back to tropes 5. “What do you mean he’s leaving PERMANENTLY,” Caelus whisper-yells.

He can’t believe it. Firstly, Mydei’s his friend now, so he can’t just leave. Secondly, how the hell is he leaving without resolving whatever he and Phainon have got going on between them?

Behind him, Dan Heng continues to redress his wounds from their fight with the Flame Reaver. One of the only reasons that they had made it out of that fight intact was because of Mydei’s godly intervention.

Mydei, who’s about to leave. Forever.

“Do you want my honest opinion?” Dan Heng asks. He doesn’t wait for Caelus to answer. “I think we should let things run their natural course.”

“There is no ‘natural course’!” Caelus wails. “He’s going to leave, and then he’ll never come back, and Phainon will be lonely forever.” He slumps backwards into Dan Heng’s arms, and ignores the resulting huff. “I know I wanted to stop being a third wheel, but not like this.”

Dan Heng sets down his bandages. “Caelus. Stop panicking,” he says firmly. “He hasn’t left yet.”

Dan Heng is right, which is why Caelus has dragged him out to find Mydei before he leaves.

For some reason, there’s a packed crowd at the Okheman gate. Caelus curses as he ducks and swerves around them. If they’re any later, they won’t be able to make it in time.

Finally, he spots Mydei at the far end of the road. He’s face to face with Phainon. They seem reluctant to look away from each other, and Caelus gets the impression that even if he called Mydei’s name, he’d go unnoticed.

“Caelus, we should—”

“Shh,” Caelus hisses, tugging Dan Heng behind a nearby pillar.

“—and I’m going to find out if the Kremnoan language is really missing that many words,” Phainon is saying.

Mydei chuckles. “The Kremnoan philosophy can never be encapsulated in a mere dictionary.”

He pauses, then. His voice softens. “But… If there’s a chance in the next life, you should come visit my library,”

Caelus claps his free hand over his mouth, and resists the urge to gasp. That is, without a doubt, the most romantic thing he’s ever heard.

“In another life, huh?” Phainon laughs, mirthlessly. His gaze drops to the floor.

The air turns cold. Caelus feels like someone stole the breath from his lungs. He grabs Dan Heng’s hand in a death grip, and after a moment, he feels Dan Heng silently squeeze back.

A complicated expression crosses Mydei’s face; some mix of regret and longing, before shifting into weary acceptance. He steps forward into Phainon’s space, deliberate and slow.

“Deliverer,” he says, voice incredibly gentle. “Phainon. Look at me.”

Phainon’s gaze stays trained on the floor. His expression is hidden by the bangs that cover his face. It’s only when Mydei lifts a gauntleted hand to gently tilt his head back, and cradles his cheek in his palms, that he looks up.

Strange, that the very same gauntlets that had caused so much destruction could caress Phainon’s cheek so carefully, like he was something precious. Mydei is a gentle man; Caelus only wishes that he realised it sooner.

“You have your duty, and I have mine,” Mydei murmurs, before leaning forward and pressing their foreheads together. A Kremnoan parting custom, Caelus recalls, from what he read in that very same textbook he had asked Mydei about.

They stay like that for a while, simply breathing together. Then, Mydei dips his head, and whispers something low in Phainon’s ear.

Caelus doesn’t hear what he says. For once, he doesn’t want to hear it, either. Somehow, he feels like he’s intruded enough.

Whatever Mydei’s words are, though, they make Phainon crumple.

“Mydei…” Phainon breathes, sounding positively heartbroken. He winds his arms around Mydei’s back and draws him impossibly closer, hands hovering near that same spot at his spine that he always seems to favour. His eyes are very bright. “You’re a cruel man, you know that?”

KISS, Caelus screams internally. KISS!!

Even Dan Heng’s invested. He’s closing his eyes and making a pained face, but his grip is deathly.

Eventually, the pair draw apart. They move slowly and reluctantly, hands lingering like they want to map every inch of the other’s skin. Finally—and to Caelus’ growing horror—Mydei tucks one stray strand of hair behind Phainon’s ear, nods, and turns around.

“May triumph always follow you, Mydeimos,” Phainon calls after him. His voice trembles, but he manages to keep it together.

Slowly, Mydei’s figure grows smaller, until he’s no bigger than a speck of crimson in the distance. Phainon waits until he’s no longer visible, before raising a hand to scrub at his eyes.

And that’s the end of that.

…

“Oh, hell no,” Caelus growls, leaping out behind the cover of the pillar. Phainon only has time to yelp, before Caelus starts to haul him away. “What do you mean, ‘in another life’—”

CAELUS’ AND DAN HENG’S INFALLIBLE 10 STEP PLAN TO STOP BEING A THIRD WHEEL  GET PHAINON AND MYDEI TOGETHER BEFORE A) CAELUS GOES CRAZY

B) THEY DIE C) BOTH??? WHY NOT THIS LIFE??????

“That sentence doesn’t even make sense anymore,” Dan Heng points out.

Caelus ignores him, and miserably adds ‘doomed yaoi’ to the tropes list.

“What is ‘yaoi’?” asks Phainon.

“Don’t worry about it,” Dan Heng tells him hastily.

Phainon leans over to inspect the whiteboard more closely. The more he reads, the higher his eyebrows climb, until Caelus starts to think that they might disappear into the snowy peaks of his hair altogether.

“Wait,” Phainon says, slowly. He’s sat cross-legged on their bedroom floor, looking slightly incredulous. “Is this what you were doing all this time?”

To his credit, Dan Heng does try to explain, but Caelus beats him to it.

“You have no idea,” Caelus tells him gravely. “No idea.”

Phainon blinks at him. He looks at the whiteboard again, and then back at Caelus, mouth agape.

“Not that I’m not flattered, but this level of detail is really quite remarkable… and slightly scary.” He pauses. “So that’s why you were trying to feel up Mydei’s chest?”

“...”

Caelus looks pointedly at the far wall. Phainon rounds on Dan Heng.

“And you were fine with that, Dan Heng?”

“I had no idea of Caelus’ plans,” Dan Heng sniffs, “because I refused to be involved in them.”

“But now you are?”

“... but now I am.”

“Stop deflecting!” Caelus cries. “Let’s get back to the topic at hand. Why did you two break up?”

“It’s hardly ‘breaking up’ if we were never together in the first place,” Phainon says, with a wry smile.

Caelus throws up his hands in disbelief. “That’s the point! Why did you never get together? You clearly care about each other, you clearly want each other—hell, half of Okhema has a betting pool going on the last time I checked—but still, you two never got together!”

“Hah! I knew there was a betting pool,” Phainon chuckles. He stretches out a leg, and grows pensive. “You’re right about the rest, though. We do care about each other.”

Then, Phainon pauses. “Actually, we did discuss whether we should announce a formal courtship, or even pin an official name to our relationship. But in the end, we decided against it.”

The admission makes Caelus’ head spin. For once, he is at a loss for words. “But why…?”

Phainon sighs, world-weary. “Mydei is fighting back the black tide as we speak. The chances of him being able to leave Castrum Kremnos are near zero. It’s a thankless battle, and he’ll keep fighting until he buckles under the burden of Strife, or until…” Phainon stops, a complicated expression crossing his face, “he no longer has to.

“That’s probably not what you wanted to hear, but it’s the truth. And I have my own duties as a Chrysos Heir. If I abandoned the Flamechase Journey for my own heart, Mydei would never let me hear the end of it.”

“Can you not visit?” Dan Heng asks.

Phainon startles. “What?”

“Castrum Kremnos. Could you not visit Mydei there?”

At that, Phainon hunches in on himself. “I’ve thought about it,” he admits. “Many a night. More than I should. But whatever the outcome, I would have to return to Okhema eventually. And with our duties, who knows when I will be able to visit Castrum Kremnos again?” He turns to gaze out of the balcony window, into the eternal dawn and beyond. “I am not so cruel a man as to reciprocate his feelings, before leaving him to be condemned to an eternity of bloodshed.”

Caelus frowns. “I don’t buy that,” he argues. “You two deserve happiness. Even if it’s fleeting. Why wait for the next life when this one’s still kicking?” He turns to his companion. “Right, Dan Heng?”

“I agree,” Dan Heng nods. “If there’s ever a chance, you should cherish those dearest to you, and hold them close now.”

Caelus feels his heart grow warm. Dan Heng, of all people, would know the most about this. If only he could explain to Phainon why.

Phainon picks at a thread on the rug. “Even if we’re fated to be apart for the rest of our days?” he asks quietly.

Caelus thinks of March, ever a steadfast companion and confidante even when he wound her up; of Welt and Himeko, who offered him a home when he had none; of Pom-Pom, who made sure to cheer him up even when he made more of a mess in the Parlor Car than help; and of Dan Heng, who has saved him more times than he can count. If Caelus lost even one of them in this lifetime without letting them know the depths of his gratitude, he’s certain that the devastation would be too much for him to bear.

“Even then,” Caelus nods. “Besides, there are far worse long-distance relationships. Mnestia and Cerces were a tree and butterfly. You literally cannot get more long distance than that.”

At that, Phainon finally laughs. It’s not like one of his pleasant facades he’d been putting on since Caelus had dragged him to their room. Instead, it’s a full laugh, right from the belly, leaving Phainon clutching his stomach as he tries to compose himself.

Caelus smiles. It’s about time he made his friend laugh properly.

“You make compelling arguments,” Phainon says, wiping his eyes. “I wonder what Mydei would say if he heard them? In all honesty, he’d probably insult me.” He climbs to his feet, and dusts off his clothes. “But… thank you. You’ve given me a lot to think about.”

Caelus claps him on the back. “Sometimes you need an outsider’s perspective,” he says, straight-faced, “before you can undoom yourselves from the narrative. And then you can put the wedding back on!”

Phainon smiles at him with the distinct air of someone who has no idea what Caelus just said, and claps him on the shoulder. “Can I ask one last question before I go?”

“Shoot.”

“May I ask why you’re so invested?” Phainon asks. “You’ve already assisted Amphoreus greatly, and while I’m immensely grateful for your assistance, I can’t help but think that we have barely anything of equivalent value to offer when it comes to matters like this.”

Caelus doesn’t miss a beat. “I need to break my curse,” he tells him, completely seriously, and refuses to respond when Phainon tries to push further.

A few days later, Phainon seeks out Caelus in the Marmoreal Market, and pulls him aside into a secluded corner.

“I’ve been thinking about what you two have told me,” Phainon says, slowly. “I think I’ve decided.”

“And…?” Caelus asks, heart in his throat.

“And I think I will visit him,” Phainon says, the corners of his mouth tugging into a smile. “It will probably be painful, and there will come a time where we’ll have to say goodbye to each other for good, but I’ve decided that’s a risk that I’m willing to take.” Phainon reaches out, and grasps Caelus’ hand. His eyes, usually so piercing, are painfully sincere. “I have to thank you and Dan Heng both, for talking some sense into me.”

“Any time,” Caelus whispers back fiercely.

The relief is so palpable that it makes Caelus feel weak in the knees. He feels weaker than when Mydei had glared at him on the roof that one time.

It’s only when Phainon has clearly rounded the corner and been gone for a few minutes that Caelus lets out a large whoop, and dashes back into his room to tell Dan Heng the good news.

Phainon departs the very next day. Caelus and Dan Heng decide to accompany him.

Once they reach the gate, however, Phainon throws out an arm and stops them from walking forward.

“One moment,” he says.

Phainon walks, leaving Caelus and Dan Heng exchanging confused glances behind. He positions himself squarely in the centre of the road and tips his head back, surveying the clear expanse of the sigh.

Phainon breathes deeply. Once, twice, and then—

“Mydeimos!” Phainon shouts, loud and clear. “Can you hear me?”

For a long moment, Caelus stays confused. He has no idea what Phainon’s doing, calling out Mydei’s full name like the man can hear him all the way from Castrum Kremnos—

BOOM.

Caelus yelps, and instinctively throws up a hand to cover his face. A beam of scarlet flashes from behind his hand and illuminates the sky. In the distance, thunder rumbles. Somehow, the sound is almost comforting.

Phainon grins, delighted. “No need to sound so confused. There’s no emergency,” he calls to the sky. The smile on his face is nearly blinding. “Just keep the front door open for me, would you? I wouldn’t want to kick it down and ruin all your hard work.”

Keep the front door open…? Oh. That would explain the red sky.

Caelus grins. That’s so sweet. The thought of Phainon summoning Mydei like an RPG god nearly brings a tear to his eye.

Phainon turns to them, sheer happiness on his face. “Thank you, my friends,” he beams. “If all goes well, I will return to Okhema in no time.”

“Wait, we’re not coming with you?” Caelus says, puzzled.

Before he can ask more questions—because after all of his plans, what do you mean they’re not going to witness the dazzling finale—Dan Heng claps a hand over his mouth.

“You’re welcome,” Dan Heng tells Phainon, even as Caelus writhes in his arms like an unruly python. “Good luck, and safe travels, Phainon.”

He waits until Phainon is just a blue blob in the distance, before letting Caelus extract himself from his grip.

“We definitely could’ve gone with him,” Caelus complains. “I wanted front row seats. I even brought popcorn.”

Dan Heng shakes his head, looking contemplative.

“I think this, of all things, is something we shouldn’t meddle in,” he says softly.

Seven days later, the masses report of Phainon’s return. Word on the street is that he returned to Okhema whistling, flushed under the perpetual daylight of the Dawn Device, and with the distinct glow of a newly courted man.

Caelus asks him to visit their room anyway. He needs to confirm that last part for himself, before he explodes out of excitement.

“So? How was it?” he asks Phainon with bated breath. If you two don’t have any juicy stories, I’m rioting, he doesn’t say.

“Good,” Phainon replies. His voice turns dreamy. “Better than good. We have an arrangement, now.” Caelus notices that his cheeks are tinted pink. Aww. “We may not have much time left, but any time I can have with him is better than nothing.”

“I’m glad you figured that out,” Caelus says, happily. “I can’t believe I’m about to say this, but I’m going to miss watching you two dance around each other.”

Phainon snickers. “Really? I was under the impression that you hated it.”

Caelus shrugs, good-naturedly. He’s just thankful he can look back on it all with rose-tinted glasses in the first place.

“On that note, may I borrow your board?” Phainon asks suddenly.

“Sure,” Caelus says, and passes it over. “What for?”

Instead of answering, Phainon stares down at the whiteboard, and uncaps the pen. His tongue sticks out of his mouth as he concentrates, and he deliberates for a minute before  decisively penning a string of words that Caelus has to crane his neck to see.

CAELUS’ AND DAN HENG’S INFALLIBLE 10 STEP PLAN TO STOP BEING A THIRD WHEEL GET PHAINON AND MYDEI TOGETHER BEFORE A) CAELUS GOES CRAZY B)

THEY DIE C) BOTH??? WHY NOT THIS LIFE??????

PHAINON’S FOOLPROOF GUIDE TO (DAN HENG) WINNING THE HEART OF

YOUR MOST DEARLY BELOVED (CAELUS)

1. “Yaoi?” (Definition to be checked!!! :D)

“I figured I should repay the favour,” Phainon says brightly. He tilts the board towards Dan Heng, just out of Caelus’ line of sight.

Dan Heng looks at it. His face goes ashen. “Absolutely not.”

For some reason, he climbs to his feet and tries to leave the room entirely. Phainon lurches forward, and manages to catch the tail of his ornaments.

“Wait! I have a track record in these things, so we can get you results in no time! Also, although Mydei pretends that he has no interest in these things, deep down he actually does, so this really is something worthwhile—”

Caelus distinctly feels like he’s missed something. “Hey, what’s on the board?” he demands. He leans over, and swipes for his whiteboard. “Hello? Hellooooo? Guys? Is there another couple I should be concerned about—?”

“Please don’t read that,” Dan Heng says, desperately.

“You can’t stop me, it’s my whiteboard,” Caelus argues back. He tugs the whiteboard out of a laughing Phainon’s hands, and turns it over—

—before watching as a jetstream of water slashes it into two clean pieces.

Caelus crosses his arms. “Seriously?”

With great shame, Dan Heng retracts his giant tail from where it’s curling around Caelus’ wrist. He lifts his hands to cover his horns, but it’s a futile effort.

“What the fuck,” says Phainon, flabbergasted. He jumps to his feet, mouth hanging wide open. His eyes look like they’re bugging out of his skull. “Wait. What—Dan Heng, are you —”

Dan Heng puts his face in his hands, and groans. Caelus, for his part, manages to stay silent for all of ten seconds, before he bursts into laughter.
